newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian bonds recover amid gloomy sentiment.
newsitem.headline: Australian bonds recover amid gloomy sentiment.

text.p: *Australian bonds closed little changed, recovering from a weak opening after two gloomy sentiment surveys kept alive thoughts of a policy easing.

Australian bonds recovered from a weak opening as two sentiment surveys for business and consumers still painted a picture of gloom, keeping alive thoughts of a further monetary policy easing, analysts said.
A sharp 12.2 percent rise in housing finance for April made little impression on the market, but the key test will be Thursday's labour force data for May.
National Australia Bank's monthly business survey showed that recent falls in interest rates had failed to arrest a decline in confidence and a generalised pick-up had yet to occur.

"Allowing for possible monthly volatility...the survey indicated continued generally lacklustre trading conditions and subdued inflation pressures - consistent with the possibility of some chance of another rate cut in coming months," economists at Bankers Trust Australia said in a report.
Meanwhile, Westpac's consumer sentiment index fell for the third successive month, dropping 2.4 percent in June to 100.0 and to its lowest level since September 1995.
The survey was the first survey since the federal budget on May 13 and the Reserve Bank's last official rate cut to 5.5 percent on May 23.

"Evidence from this survey indicates that for the time being unemployment may have taken over from interest rates as the most important influence on consumer sentiment," Westpac's General Manager of Economics, Bill Evans, said.

If this is the case, consumers will get little joy from Thursday's May jobs data. Economists expect the figures to show unemployment remaining at 8.7 percent with only a moderate rise of 15,000 jobs for the month, according to a Reuters survey.
The huge jump in housing finance was in line with expectations and was seen as having no implications for monetary policy at this stage, economists said.

("However) continued improvement in the housing sector will flow through to other industries and assist the economy achieving the government's growth target for 1997/98," said Hans Kunnen, chief economist at Colonial State Bank.

The market got off on a soft footing, largely mirroring Tuesday's close in U.S. Treasuries. Turnover was boosted by roll-over of futures contracts to September from June with bills closing out on Thursday and three and 10-year bonds on Monday.
The market continued to be outpaced by Canada, which closed strong on foreign buying and spread narrowing trades to the U.S.
Canada, like other dollar bloc markets in recent days, has been benefitting from a safe-haven status for European investors amid uncertainty over the EMU, analysts said.
